analysis.one_liner: Lets the labor board reinstate and compensate workers punished for unfair-labor-practice strikes.
analysis.headline: A bill to give striking workers reinstatement and back pay remedies died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the National Labor Relations Act so that when an employer punishes a worker for joining a lawful strike over the employer's own unfair labor practices, the National Labor Relations Board could order the worker reinstated, require back pay, and require the employer to post a notice committing to observe worker rights. It was introduced by Representative Pete Stauber, a Republican from Minnesota, and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee. The committee never acted on it, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who strike to protest their employer's unfair labor practices, such as firing or disciplining union supporters. If such a worker is fired or otherwise punished for striking, the NLRB could order the employer to take them back, pay them lost wages, and post a public notice of its duty to respect worker rights.

how_it_helps.text: Amends Section 10(c) of the National Labor Relations Act to expressly authorize the NLRB to order reinstatement of an employee it finds was discriminated against for participating in a lawful strike protesting an employer's unfair labor practice [S2][S3].
The same provision lets the Board require back pay, a posted notice of the employer's commitment to employee rights, and other affirmative action it considers appropriate [S2][S3].
The bill states as congressional policy that workers have the right to participate in lawful strikes protesting unfair labor practices [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who retaliate against striking workers would bear the cost of reinstatement orders, back pay, and compliance notices. The cost falls only on employers the Board finds acted unlawfully.

drawbacks.text: The remedy is narrow: it applies only to strikes protesting an employer's unfair labor practices, not to the more common economic strikes over wages and conditions, so most striking workers would see no change [S2][S3].
Employers and business groups generally argue that stronger strike remedies raise labor costs and encourage longer strikes; the bill imposes no offsetting limits on strike conduct.

The NLRB already has broad authority to order reinstatement and back pay for unfair labor practices under existing Section 10(c), so the amendment largely makes explicit what the Board can generally already do, limiting its practical effect [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a modest, targeted change: it helps a specific group of strikers get their jobs and wages back when an employer breaks the law, at a cost only to employers found to have broken the law. Its main weakness is its narrowness and the fact that it largely restates remedies the Board already has, so it is more a statement of policy than a major new protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Pete Stauber introduced the bill on May 19, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S1][S5].
No other member of the House cosponsored it; the cosponsor list stayed at zero [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point in the 117th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: employers retain the existing legal landscape for responding to strikes, and no new remedies were created for workers punished for striking. With no cosponsors and no committee action, no one lobbied this bill forward or blocked it visibly; it simply never drew the support needed to move.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, whose legal position is unchanged

for.name: Rep. Pete Stauber
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Education and Labor Committee.

against.name: Rep. Robert C. 'Bobby' Scott
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsored the bill and no member of either party signed on, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition shows up in the record.

industries.note: Under the bill, employers found to have punished workers for protesting the employer's unfair labor practices could be ordered to reinstate them and pay back wages. The bill died, so employers face no new obligations.
The bill would have given union members and other workers a clearer statutory remedy when employers retaliate against strikers, reinforcing the right to strike. It never advanced.

The bill would have written the Board's authority to reinstate and compensate discriminated strikers explicitly into the statute. It died, leaving the Board's existing general remedial authority unchanged.
